description: F-9: the input contract of the operations, pinned where it is decided — the same JSON call must be refused the same way in every implementation. It is the write-side twin of `parameter-contract`, and the asymmetry it closes was the wrong way round: every projection parameter had been declared since 0.7, and `execute()` read what it recognised and ignored the rest. So a typo in a READ failed loudly, and a typo in a WRITE was silence plus a default — and the write is the one that ends up in the books. Four rules, each with its own defect behind it. (1) An undeclared input is a caller mistake: `usefulLifeYears` looks right, means nothing, and left the pack's lookup in charge of a useful life the caller believed they had set — summae's own audit-trail test passed it for months without a word. (2) A number sent as a string is rejected rather than dropped: every handler read `typeof value === 'number'`, so a form's "30" did not fail, it VANISHED, and the documented default stood in its place. (3) An amount is Money, not a number: `proceeds: 2000` was read with an is-object check and silently became 'no proceeds', booking a disposal as if the asset had been scrapped for nothing. (4) Absent is not wrong — an omitted optional input keeps its documented default, and null counts as omitted. Deliberately NOT enforced here: `required`. An operation missing its subject already fails with a better code than this layer could give (E_VOUCHER_UNKNOWN, E_ASSET_UNKNOWN); the finding is about inputs that are present and wrong.

expect.comment: The near miss: it is called usefulLifeMonths. Before the contract the asset was created — with the pack's 36 months, not the caller's five years, and nothing said which of the two had won.
The same call with the declared name goes through.
A form posts strings. The year was read with a number check, so it was not rejected but ignored, and the run silently used its default year of 0 — a run that touched nothing and reported success.

An amount is Money — an object with a decimal amount as a STRING. Passed as a JSON number it failed the is-object check and became 'no proceeds': the disposal booked the full carrying amount as a loss, as if the machine had been scrapped rather than sold for 2000.00.
Absent is not wrong: an omitted optional input keeps its documented default, and null counts as omitted — JSON callers and CLI wrappers write it both ways.

Only the accepted calls are in the books: acquisition 3600.00, depreciation to the disposal month 900.00 (nine plan months), write-off of the remaining 2700.00 against 2000.00 proceeds, so 700.00 of loss. The four refused calls left no trace at all — a refusal that had already written something would be worse than the silence it replaces.
